name: Methylene blue megadosing

image.caption: Reflections in a flask of Methylene Blue

lead:
Methylene blue is a blue dye first made in 1876 that is also an approved medicine for methemoglobinemia. Some online communities, including looksmax.org and biohacking circles, take it at high amounts hoping for more energy, sharper focus and better-looking, healthier skin through improved cellular energy.
The appearance payoff is claimed and indirect: proponents describe a chain of mitochondrial support, more energy and drive, better training and sleep, and a younger look. Clinical research covers its approved medical uses and a few neuropsychiatric trials with mixed results; none has measured appearance.

paras: Accounts describe oral drops or solutions bought as lab or aquarium-grade products, and sometimes topical use. Users commonly stack it with other nootropics, which makes it hard to attribute effects. Many report an early boost that fades. Specific amounts are not given here.

Methylene blue inhibits monoamine oxidase, and combining it with SSRIs or other serotonergic drugs can cause serotonin syndrome. It can cause hemolysis in people with G6PD deficiency, turns urine blue-green, and stains teeth and surfaces. Product quality varies outside pharmacy channels, and its use for anti-aging or cognition is not approved.

Claimed support for mitochondrial energy and mood
angle.text: Proponents say methylene blue boosts cellular energy and focus, which they link to better training, sleep and skin. This chain is based on user accounts and early lab concepts; no study has measured appearance outcomes.

lead: Methylene blue megadosing is a practice in forums and biohacking circles of taking methylene blue, a synthetic blue dye and prescription medicine, at amounts well above its clinical context, for claimed gains in energy, mood, focus and skin health [1][2]. People pursuing it frame it as a route to looking younger and more vital: more cellular energy, better drive for training and sleep, and healthier-looking skin.

Methylene blue was first prepared by Heinrich Caro in 1876, was used against malaria by Paul Guttmann and Paul Ehrlich in 1891, and today is mainly a treatment for methemoglobinemia, where it restores oxygen-carrying hemoglobin [3][2]. It is also used in some vasoplegic and septic shock settings [4][5].

Online enthusiasm includes looksmax.org threads where users describe feeling mentally sharp and energized after starting it [6], a Hacker News discussion of what the compound can and cannot do for the brain [7], and social-media promotion for anti-aging and cognition, which Wikipedia notes lacks scientific consensus or regulatory approval for those uses [2].
infobox: Synthetic dye; MAO inhibitor; redox agent
Intravenous (medical); oral and topical use reported online

paras: Methylene blue (methylthioninium chloride) is used as a stain, indicator and medicine. Caro prepared it in 1876, Guttmann and Ehrlich used it against malaria in 1891, and Matilda Brooks reported its role as a cyanide antidote in 1933 [2]. It is best known as an antidote for acquired methemoglobinemia and has been extended to ifosfamide neurotoxicity and refractory vasoplegic shock [3].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and biohacking communities
paras: On looksmax.org, one user describes feeling young again with a sharp brain and strong drive after using a methylene blue product [6]; another thread announces plans to megadose it [8]. Replies ask whether it is taken orally or applied topically, showing mixed routes of use [6].

In a 2025 Hacker News thread on the compound and the brain, commenters said users often report an initial benefit that fades, noted that it is difficult to blind because it turns urine blue, and raised safety warnings about serotonin syndrome and G6PD deficiency [7]. Some commenters were skeptical, attributing reported effects to placebo or to stacking with other supplements [7].

Trials concern medical uses. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of six randomized trials (302 patients) in septic shock found methylene blue may reduce short-term mortality and hospital stay, with low certainty [9]. Reviews describe its use in vasoplegia and methemoglobinemia [4][5][3]. Wikipedia reports mixed results in trials for bipolar depression, Alzheimer's disease and schizophrenia [2]. No clinical study has examined high-amount use for skin, energy or appearance in healthy people.

Common effects include headache, nausea and blue-green urine [10][2]. Because methylene blue inhibits monoamine oxidase, high intravenous amounts combined with SSRIs or other serotonergic drugs have caused serotonin syndrome, and hemolytic anemia is a concern in G6PD deficiency [2]. A Hacker News commenter described a death linked to home use for depression, which could not be verified [7]. Wikipedia advises use only under a doctor's prescription [2].
